name: Functional analysis
description: For business analysts documenting what an application does, independent of the technology it is built with. Gives functional areas, use cases, screen descriptions, use case diagrams and screen flows.
author: B2IT

personas.name: Analysis
personas.description: The business analyst. Everything here is technology independent: what the application does and why, in terms that stay true whatever it is built with, and after any rewrite. No module names, no class names, no control names, no table names.

node_types.name: Functional area
node_types.description: A group of use cases that belong together for the business, for example orders, customers, invoicing, or users and sign-in. The analyst's tree is browsed by these, so every use case sits in exactly one of them. The folder itself carries the overview of its area.

node_types.name: Use case
node_types.description: One thing a user can achieve with the application, written so it would still be true if the application were rebuilt in any language. When it is derived from existing screens and code, it is never phrased in their terms: no module names, no class names, no control names, no table names. A screen that only exists to pick a value for another screen is a step of that use case, not a use case of its own.

fields.name: actor
fields.label: Actor
fields.hint: Who carries it out, as a role rather than a person or a form.

fields.name: goal
fields.label: Goal
fields.hint: What the actor is trying to achieve, in business terms.

fields.name: trigger
fields.label: Trigger
fields.hint: What makes it start: a decision, an event, a schedule.

fields.name: preconditions
fields.label: Preconditions
fields.hint: What has to be true before it can run, including who is allowed to.

fields.name: main_flow
fields.label: Main flow
fields.hint: The normal course as numbered steps, one step per thing the actor or the system does. Say what happens, not which control is clicked.

fields.name: alternate_flows
fields.label: Alternate flows
fields.hint: The variations and what happens when it goes wrong, each with the condition that leads into it.

fields.name: business_rules
fields.label: Business rules
fields.hint: The rules the system enforces here, written so they could be handed to a developer who has never seen the existing code.

fields.name: data
fields.label: Data involved
fields.hint: The business things it reads and changes, in business words. A customer, an order, a role: not a table.

fields.name: outcome
fields.label: Outcome
fields.hint: What is true once it has finished, including what the user is told.

fields.name: open_questions
fields.label: Open questions
fields.hint: What the code did not make clear. Put it here rather than inventing an intent; this is the list the analyst takes to the business.

node_types.name: Screen description
node_types.description: One screen as the business analyst sees it: what a user comes to it for, what it shows and what it lets them do, written so it would still be true after a rewrite. When it is derived from an existing screen, it is never phrased in its terms: no module names, no class names, no control names, no table names. A dialog that only exists to pick a value for another screen is described as part of the screen that opens it, not as a screen of its own.

fields.name: use_case
fields.label: Use case
fields.hint: The use case this screen is a step of, by its exact title. When it serves several, give each title separated by "; ".

fields.name: purpose
fields.label: Purpose
fields.hint: What the user comes to this screen to do, in business terms.

fields.name: users
fields.label: Used by
fields.hint: Who works with it, as roles rather than people or logins.

fields.name: information_shown
fields.label: Information shown
fields.hint: What the user sees, as business information: which customer, which order, which totals. Not fields, grids or tabs.

fields.name: user_actions
fields.label: What the user can do
fields.hint: Each thing the user can do here and what it achieves. Say what happens, not which button is clicked.

fields.name: navigation
fields.label: Comes from / leads to
fields.hint: Where the user arrives from and where they can go next, as steps in their work rather than menu paths.

fields.name: rules
fields.label: Rules the user meets
fields.hint: What is mandatory, what is refused and what the user is told, in words a developer could implement without the existing code.

fields.name: open_questions
fields.label: Open questions
fields.hint: What the code did not make clear. Put it here rather than inventing an intent.

node_types.name: Use case diagram
node_types.description: A picture of who uses the system for what: the actors (job positions, outside parties) and the use cases they take part in, grouped by functional area, with how the use cases depend on each other (include, extend, one leading into the next). Drawn from the use case topics it shows, in the business's words, so a reader sees the whole before opening one use case.

fields.name: scope
fields.label: Scope
fields.hint: What it covers: a functional area by its name, or "the whole system".

fields.name: overview
fields.label: Overview
fields.hint: What the diagram shows and what it leaves out, in a few sentences.

fields.name: actors
fields.label: Actors
fields.hint: A table: each actor, who that is in the business, and what they may do.

fields.name: diagram
fields.label: Diagram
fields.hint: A PlantUML use case diagram: actors on the left, the use cases by their exact titles inside the system boundary, one package per functional area (use cases from neighbouring areas in grey), <<include>>/<<extend>> where one use case depends on another. A sentence before it says how to read it.

fields.name: notes
fields.label: Notes
fields.hint: What the picture cannot say: rules about who may do what, gaps and open questions about roles — a subsection each.

node_types.name: Screen flow
node_types.description: How a user moves between the screens: where each screen is reached from, which action leads where, and where the user ends up after signing out or finishing a task. Drawn from the screen description topics (their "comes from / leads to"), so a reader sees the whole application, or one journey through it, at a glance.

fields.name: scope
fields.label: Scope
fields.hint: What it covers: "the whole application", or a journey ("placing and invoicing an order").

fields.name: overview
fields.label: Overview
fields.hint: Where the flow starts, the main routes through it, and what it leaves out.

fields.name: screens
fields.label: Screens
fields.hint: A table: each screen in the flow, who uses it, and its screen description.

fields.name: flow
fields.label: Flow
fields.hint: A Mermaid flowchart: one node per screen by its name, its functional area under the name, coloured by who uses it, each arrow labelled with the user action (or the condition) that takes the user there; dotted arrows for routes that are offered but broken. A sentence before it says how to read it.

fields.name: notes
fields.label: Notes
fields.hint: What the picture cannot say: dead ends, lost data on leaving, open questions about navigation — a subsection each.
